title: Making plans together
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: -(eu)llae-yo IS THE INVITATION ENDING and L1 named it as deferred; plans are what it is for. gachi bap meogeullae-yo? is the everyday Korean invitation, and it differs from a plain question exactly as English "shall we" differs from "will you" — it asks the listener's WISH rather than a fact. No second future is opened here: L1-M6's -l geoyeyo carries the plan itself, -gess- stays deferred, and -(eu)psida belongs to the -mnida level and travels with it, so it is named in usage and never written.

THE CLOCK IS WHERE M5'S NUMBER RULE PAYS FOR ITSELF IN ONE BREATH: the HOUR is a native number with the counter -si, and the MINUTES are a Sino number with -bun. du si samsip bun is half past two, and it uses both systems in four syllables. There is no rule beyond the one M5 stated — which is the point of putting them side by side.

The days are a closed set built on ONE ROOT: woryoil, hwayoil, suyoil, mogyoil, geumyoil, toyoil, iryoil, where -yoil is the shared ending. Seven words cost about two, and a learner shown the pattern will not memorise seven. L1-M7's -e marks the day as well as the hour — woryoil-e, du si-e — a fourth job for one particle and no new row for any of it.

Plans are made among friends, and here THIS COURSE MOVES THE OPPOSITE WAY FROM THE OTHER EIGHT. There is no informal tier to switch into, because banmal is not written in en-ko L2 at all — so the module stays neutral throughout and the friendliness is carried by the ENDING (-(eu)llae-yo rather than an honorific imperative) and by gachi. An author who has read the other L2 briefs will look for an informal chip; it is deliberately absent.

joayo does a second job here — L1-M9's "is good" is also "sounds good", which is how a Korean accepts a plan — and geuraeyo ("let's do that") settles it. Neither opens a new row for the acceptance: joayo stays L1-M9's, and geuraeyo is the one fresh word the exchange needs.

sentences.cue: Shall we get something to eat?

words.note: Written with a t and said with a ch, which is one of Korean's regular sound changes. It is the word that turns any verb into an invitation.
L1-M3's meokda with the invitation ending. It asks what the listener WANTS rather than what they will do, which is why it is an offer and not a question.

sentences.trap: bap is rice and it is also 'a meal'. Gachi bap meogeullae-yo? does not propose rice specifically — it is the ordinary Korean way to suggest eating anything at all together.
sentences.sound: GA-chi bap meo-geul-LAE-yo. gachi is written gat-i and said ga-chi.

variations.changed: without gachi, so it asks about them rather than about both of you

mistake.why: An invitation takes the -llae-yo ending: Gachi bap meogeullae-yo?

sentences.usage: The commonest invitation in the language, and it means far more than the food.
sentences.mnemonic: -llae-yo asks what you WANT, not what you will do.

words.note: geum, gold, plus -yoil. All seven days share that ending and differ by one syllable, so seven words cost about two.
Time in the sense of free time, and also an hour's duration. Korean asks whether you HAVE time, exactly as English does.

sentences.trap: -e marks the day here, and it is the same particle that marks a place in L1-M7 and an hour in S04. One particle, four jobs, and Korean sees no difficulty in that at all.
sentences.sound: GEU-myo-i-re SI-gan i-SSEO-yo. The l of geumyoil runs into the particle as an r.

variations.changed: L1-M6's tomorrow, which takes no particle

mistake.why: A named day takes -e: Geumyoil-e sigan isseoyo?

words.note: wol, moon, plus -yoil — the same Monday the English word is. hwa is fire, su is water, mok is wood, and the week is the old planets in order.
mannada, to meet, with the invitation ending. Unlike M2's Korean it needs no reflexive pronoun — you simply meet a person.

sentences.trap: Meeting takes no extra pronoun in Korean. English says 'meet up' and Spanish and Korean both simply meet, so nothing goes between mannallae-yo and the day.
sentences.sound: WO-ryo-i-re man-nal-LAE-yo. The nn of mannada is held.

mistake.why: A named day takes -e: Woryoil-e mannallae-yo?

sentences.usage: Proposing the day, once you know they are free.
sentences.mnemonic: Moon, fire, water, wood — the week is the old planets.

sentences.cue: Let's meet at half past two.

words.note: The hour counter, and the number in front of it is NATIVE: han si, du si, se si. It is M5's law in its first four syllables.
The minute counter, and the number in front of it is SINO: sip bun, samsip bun. One clock, two number systems, and no exception either way.

sentences.trap: du si samsip bun uses BOTH number systems in one phrase — native for the hour, Sino for the minutes — and getting it the other way round is the mistake M5's rule exists to prevent.
sentences.sound: du si sam-SIP bu-ne man-NA-yo. samsip is two even syllables.

variations.changed: on the hour, with no minutes

variations.cue: Let's meet at ten past three.
variations.changed: a different time, same two systems

mistake.why: The hour takes a native number: Du si samsip bun-e mannayo.

sentences.usage: Settling the time, which in Korea happens fast.
sentences.mnemonic: Native hour. Sino minute. Every time.

words.note: The question word for a time, and a sibling of L1-M9's wae and L1-M8's myeot. Like every question word it takes no topic particle.

sentences.trap: L1-M6's -l geoyeyo carries the plan and nothing else is needed. Korean has a second future in -gess-, and this level does not open it; a learner who meets it later will find it does a different job.
sentences.sound: EON-je gal GEO-ye-yo. eonje is two even syllables with no stress.

variations.changed: asking about time rather than a plan

mistake.why: A question word never takes the topic particle: Eonje gal geoyeyo?

sentences.usage: Pinning down a plan somebody has mentioned in passing.
sentences.mnemonic: Question words take no topic. Ever.

words.note: From geureohda, 'to be so'. It agrees, it settles a plan, and with a rising tone it asks 'really?' — three jobs, decided by the tone.

sentences.trap: joayo here is not describing anything. L1-M9 taught it as 'is good' and this is its second job — 'sounds good' — which is how a Korean accepts a proposal, and no new word is needed for it.
sentences.sound: JO-a-yo, geu-RAE-yo. The h inside joayo is silent.

variations.changed: on its own, which is enough
the same word as a question

mistake.why: Accepting a plan takes joayo: Joayo, geuraeyo.

sentences.usage: Accepting — and in Korea it is said quickly.

words.note: One word for an appointment, an arrangement with a friend and a promise. Yaksok isseoyo is the polite way to say you are busy without saying with what.

sentences.trap: yaksok isseoyo declines an invitation without giving a reason, and nobody will ask for one. Korean treats an existing arrangement as a complete answer, where English often expects a detail.
sentences.sound: TO-yo-i-re YAK-sok i-SSEO-yo. The k of yaksok is unreleased.

variations.cue: I have nothing on on Saturday.

variations.changed: with the subject particle spelled out

mistake.why: Having something takes isseoyo: Toyoil-e yaksok isseoyo.

sentences.usage: Declining without explaining, which is complete in Korean.
sentences.mnemonic: yaksok isseoyo is a whole answer.

words.note: The question word with the SUBJECT particle, exactly as M3's nuga was. Asking which time is good is asking which time is the subject of 'is good'.

words.cue: how about it? · how is it?
words.note: The whole of "how about …?", and it comes after what it asks about: Toyoil-eun eottaeyo? It is also the ordinary way to ask how something was.

sentences.trap: joayo does its 'suits you' job here, which L1-M9 named and this module uses twice. Nothing about the sentence says 'you' — the question alone carries it.
sentences.sound: EON-je-ga JO-a-yo. The two words run together.

variations.changed: the answer, with the day as subject
a suggestion, with the topic particle contrasting
a time rather than a day

mistake.why: A question word takes the subject particle: Eonje-ga joayo?

sentences.usage: Handing the choice to the other person.
sentences.mnemonic: joayo suits you, and never needs a 'you'.

words.note: The plain -yo form does duty as a gentle 'let's' when the plan is already agreed. -(eu)psida would be the formal version and belongs to the -mnida level this course does not write.

sentences.trap: -eseo and not -e, because meeting is something that HAPPENS at the station rather than a place you are going to. M4's law again, in a sentence about plans.
sentences.sound: YEO-ge-seo man-NA-yo. The k of yeok softens into the particle.

variations.cue: Let's meet at the bus stop.
Let's meet at the station at two.

variations.changed: -e, because going there is a destination

sentences.usage: Settling where, once when is settled.

words.note: The plain -yo of boda, to see, doing duty as a farewell that promises a meeting. Its -l shape bol is what M1's ability question takes.

sentences.trap: bwayo promises the meeting, exactly as a day after 'see you' does in English. L1-M2's annyeonghi gaseyo is the goodbye with nothing attached, and the two are not interchangeable once a plan exists.
sentences.sound: geu-RAE-yo, GEU-myo-i-re BWA-yo. bwayo is one syllable and a half.

variations.changed: a time instead of a day

mistake.why: A named day takes -e: Geuraeyo, geumyoil-e bwayo.

sentences.usage: Closing the conversation once the plan is fixed.
sentences.mnemonic: bwayo promises. annyeonghi gaseyo does not.

comprehensionPool.cue: Shall we get something to eat?
Let's meet at half past two.
